entities: nearly every function of the cell

triples.head: genes
triples.evidence: Genes are composed of DNA and are linearly arranged on chromosomes.

triples.head: genes
triples.evidence: Genes specify the sequences of amino acids, which are the building blocks of proteins.

triples.head: proteins
triples.tail: nearly every function of the cell
triples.evidence: proteins are responsible for orchestrating nearly every function of the cell.

triples.head: transcription
triples.evidence: The cellular process of transcription generates messenger RNA (mRNA), a mobile molecular copy of one or more genes with an alphabet of A, C, G, and uracil (U).

triples.head: mRNA
triples.evidence: Translation of the mRNA template on ribosomes converts nucleotide-based genetic information into a protein product.

triples.head: DNA
triples.evidence: The flow of genetic information in cells from DNA to mRNA to protein is described by the central dogma, which states that genes specify the sequence of mRNAs, which in turn specify the sequence of amino acids making up all proteins.

triples.head: mRNA
triples.evidence: The flow of genetic information in cells from DNA to mRNA to protein is described by the central dogma, which states that genes specify the sequence of mRNAs, which in turn specify the sequence of amino acids making up all proteins.

triples.head: DNA
triples.evidence: The copying of DNA to RNA is relatively straightforward, with one nucleotide being added to the mRNA strand for every nucleotide read in the DNA strand.

triples.head: mRNA
triples.evidence: The translation to protein is still systematic and colinear, such that nucleotides 1 to 3 correspond to amino acid 1, nucleotides 4 to 6 correspond to amino acid 2, and so on.

triples.head: codons
triples.evidence: Each amino acid is defined by a three-nucleotide sequence called the triplet codon.

triples.head: codons
triples.evidence: Scientists theorized that amino acids were encoded by nucleotide triplets and that the genetic code was “degenerate.”

triples.head: AUG
triples.evidence: Another codon, AUG, also has a special function. In addition to specifying the amino acid methionine, it also serves as the start codon to initiate translation.

triples.head: AUG
triples.evidence: Another codon, AUG, also has a special function. In addition to specifying the amino acid methionine, it also serves as the start codon to initiate translation.

triples.head: nonsense codons
triples.evidence: In addition to codons that instruct the addition of a specific amino acid to a polypeptide chain, three of the 64 codons terminate protein synthesis and release the polypeptide from the translation machinery.

triples.head: genetic code
triples.evidence: The genetic code is nearly universal. With a few minor exceptions, virtually all species use the same genetic code for protein synthesis.
